subject: mathematics
question_text: If f: A→B, g: B→C are two bijective functions then prove that gof: A→C is also a bijective function.

mark_split.label: Proof that gof is one one

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove that gof is bijective — name the two things you have to prove, and say how each proof goes.

steps.label: Write what is given
steps.margin_note: This earns no mark by itself, but it names the two properties the whole proof uses. Write it first so every later step has something to point back to.
lines: f: A→B and g: B→C are bijective functions.
So f and g are both one one and onto.

lines.text: To prove: gof: A→C is bijective, that is,

lines: gof is one one and gof is onto.

recall.must_convey: That f and g are given as bijections, and that a bijection means both one one and onto. Saying only 'they are bijective' without unpacking it into one one and onto is partial — confidence 0.5 or lower.

steps.why: The proof has exactly two halves because bijective means exactly two things. Naming them at the start tells the examiner you know what has to be shown.
common_mistakes: Starting the algebra without saying what has to be proved.
Writing 'f and g are bijective' but never using one one and onto separately.

steps.label: Prove gof is one one
steps.margin_note: Three of the seven marks. Take two elements with the same image and work backwards through g first, then f. Quote the reason in brackets at each step — the reasons are what the examiner marks.

lines.text: (i) To prove gof: A→C is one one

lines: ⇒ f(a₁) = f(a₂)   (∵ g is one one)
⇒ a₁ = a₂   (∵ f is one one)

recall.must_convey: Set (gof)(a₁) = (gof)(a₂), remove g first because g is one one, then remove f because f is one one, and conclude a₁ = a₂. Both reasons must be spoken, and g must come before f.

steps.why: One one means different inputs never share an output. The clean way to show it is to assume two inputs DO share an output and be forced to conclude they were the same input all along.
common_mistakes: Peeling off f before g — the outer function is g, so g comes off first.
Writing the chain with no reasons in brackets; the reasons carry the marks.
Claiming gof is one one because f and g are, without the argument.

steps.label: Prove gof is onto
steps.margin_note: Four of the seven marks — the bigger half. Start from any c in C and walk backwards: g onto gives you b, then f onto gives you a. Finish by showing that this a really does map to c.

lines.text: (ii) To prove gof: A→C is onto

lines: g: B→C is onto, so for every c ∈ C there
is b ∈ B with g(b) = c   …(1)
f: A→B is onto, so for this b ∈ B there
is a ∈ A with f(a) = b   …(2)
So for every c ∈ C there is a ∈ A with

recall.must_convey: Start from an arbitrary c in C, use g onto to get b in B with g(b) = c, then use f onto to get a in A with f(a) = b, then show (gof)(a) = c. The order matters: c gives b, b gives a.

steps.why: Onto means nothing in C is left out. So you must be able to start at ANY c and produce an a that reaches it — which is why the proof runs backwards, from c to b to a.
common_mistakes: Starting from a in A instead of from c in C; that proves nothing about coverage.
Using f onto first — you have no b to feed it until g gives you one.
Stopping at f(a) = b without showing that (gof)(a) = c.

steps.label: Conclude bijective
steps.margin_note: No separate mark, but write it. The question asked for bijective, so the last line must say bijective — both halves named together.
lines: gof: A→C is one one and onto.
∴ gof: A→C is a bijective function.

recall.must_convey: That gof is bijective BECAUSE it was shown to be both one one and onto. The two halves must be tied to the conclusion.

steps.why: The question used the word bijective, so the answer must end on that word. An examiner reading only your last line should see the question answered.
common_mistakes: Ending at 'onto' and never writing the word bijective.
Writing only 'hence proved' with nothing named.
